This time 15 more anti-aircraft systems had been purchased, along with a small military jet. Supreme leader Falah Madhir made his way out into the hostile desert landscape, ready to receive the supplies. After 10 minutes of waiting, 2 large trucks came into view. [b]Cyber Unit - Fort Verdigo 19th March 2025 [/b]

I stared intently at the glowing monitor in the dimly lit room, my fingers tapping rhythmically on the keyboard as the encrypted data from our reconnaissance drones streamed in. Each line of text tightened the knot in my stomach furtheranother successful arms shipment had reached the Sal-Baliz. This wasn't routine intel; this could change the entire strategic picture.

"Fifteen advanced anti-aircraft systems confirmed delivered. One military jet identified. Visual confirmation of Supreme Leader Falah Madhir present at delivery," I muttered aloud, double-checking the data feeds. The coordinates were clear, a remote desert region previously marked as inactivenow a significant threat.

My heartbeat quickened. I knew our air force was planning another raid in less than 48 hours. Without this intel, they'd fly straight into a trap.

Quickly, I compiled the images and encrypted reports, swiftly initiating the secure uplink. My screen flashed green: Connection established. I paused momentarily, considering the gravity of the message I was about to send.

"High priority intel. Sal-Baliz faction acquisition of advanced AA systems and aerial assets confirmed. Immediate threat to planned air operations. Recommend mission reassessment."

With a decisive keystroke, the data packet surged upward through our secured channels, speeding toward Air Defense Command.

But I knew too well how bureaucracy moved within the ranks. First, the message would hit the regional intel supervisor, who would forward it to the area commander, who then would escalate it to the district operations center. From there, another set of eyes would check and confirm before it moved upward to headquarters, through at least six more layers of military analysts and command officers, each scrutinizing the intel before finallyhopefullyreaching the Air Force strategic planning division.

Each handover risked delay, misinterpretation, or even outright dismissal as the intel was handed from one officer to the next. I leaned back, exhaling deeply, frustration bubbling beneath my calm exterior. With every minute that ticked by, the intel risked becoming outdatedor worse, arriving too late to save our pilots from flying blindly into the Sal-Baliz trap.

Now it was out of my hands. All I could do was wait and hope Command understood the urgency in time.
